title: Fair and efficient division
description: Allocations of indivisible goods that are envy-free and Pareto-efficient; existence is Sigma-2-complete even for additive values (de Keijzer, Bouveret, Klos and Zhang). The abstraction guesses an envy-free allocation and the check one that dominates it. Being dominated depends on sums, which a clause cannot say, so the refinement is a rule (Shape 3): no later candidate may be dominated by this counterexample.

fragments.name: shared
fragments.description: Agents, goods and values. Added to every solver.
fragments.text: % The instance (its facts) is in the Instances tab.

fragments.name: abstraction
fragments.text:
% A candidate: every good goes to one agent ...
1 { gets(A,G) : agent(A) } 1 :- good(G).
% ... and nobody envies anybody: A does not value B's bundle more than the own one.
:- agent(A), agent(B), A != B,
   #sum { V,G : gets(B,G), value(A,G,V) ; -V,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) } > 0.
#show gets/2.

fragments.name: refine
fragments.description: Grounded once per counterexample: later candidates must not be dominated by it.
fragments.text:
#program refine(k).
% cex(k,alt(A,G)): in the k-th counterexample agent A gets good G.
% loses(k,A) / gains(k,A): agent A is worse / better off there than in the candidate.
loses(k,A) :- agent(A),
    #sum { V,G : cex(k,alt(A,G)), value(A,G,V) ; -V,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) } < 0.
gains(k,A) :- agent(A),
    #sum { V,G : cex(k,alt(A,G)), value(A,G,V) ; -V,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) } > 0.
% The candidate must not be dominated by it: if somebody gains, somebody loses.
:- gains(k,A), not loses(k,B) : agent(B).

fragments.name: glue
fragments.description: The interface atoms: who gets what.

fragments.name: check
fragments.description: Looks for an allocation that Pareto-dominates the candidate (solver C).
fragments.text:
% A counterexample: another allocation (it need not be envy-free) in which ...
1 { alt(A,G) : agent(A) } 1 :- good(G).
% ... nobody is worse off ...
:- agent(A), #sum { V,G : alt(A,G), value(A,G,V) ; -V,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) } < 0.
% ... and somebody is better off.
gains(A) :- agent(A), #sum { V,G : alt(A,G), value(A,G,V) ; -V,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) } > 0.
better :- gains(A).
:- not better.
#show alt/2.
% No relevant/1 rules: the loop passes the allocation alt/2 to the refine part.

fragments.name: welfare
fragments.text:
% A Pareto-optimal counterexample: of the allocations that dominate the candidate, the check
% returns one of maximum total value. It is Pareto-optimal (an allocation that dominated it would
% dominate the candidate too, with a larger total), so its rule "not dominated by this one" removes
% as much as a dominance rule can (variant optimal-counterexample).
#maximize { V,A,G : alt(A,G), value(A,G,V) }.

fragments.name: allocation
fragments.text:
% A candidate without envy-freeness: every good goes to one agent. Envy is found by a check of
% its own (fragment envy) and refined lazily, one envious pair at a time.
1 { gets(A,G) : agent(A) } 1 :- good(G).
#show gets/2.

fragments.name: envy
fragments.text:
% A counterexample to envy-freeness: agent X values the bundle of Y more than its own.
1 { envy(X,Y) : agent(X), agent(Y), X != Y } 1.
:- envy(X,Y), #sum { V,G : gets(Y,G), value(X,G,V) ; -V,G : gets(X,G), value(X,G,V) } <= 0.
% Envy depends only on the bundles of X and Y: every allocation that gives them the same bundles
% has the same envy. So the clause says that one of their goods must move.
relevant(gets(Z,G)) :- envy(X,Y), good(G), Z = (X;Y).
#show envy/2.

fragments.name: welfare_a
fragments.text:
% Envy-free allocations of the largest total value first: they are the most likely to be
% Pareto-optimal, so the first checks fail and the counterexamples come later.
#maximize { V,A,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) }.

fragments.name: algorithm1
fragments.text:
% Algorithm 1 of Conati, Niskanen, de Haan and Jarvisalo (AAMAS 2025), for additive values.
#program climb(k).
% cand(k,T): the k-th candidate of a climb (cand_false(k,T): T is false in it). up(k), assumed by
% the loop for one solve, asks for an envy-free allocation that dominates it: nobody is worse
% off, somebody better off (lines 7-10 of Algorithm 1; there: happy agents stay happy, one more).
{ up(k) }.
worse(k,A) :- agent(A),
    #sum { V,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) ; -V,G : cand(k,gets(A,G)), not cand_false(k,gets(A,G)), value(A,G,V) } < 0.
better(k,A) :- agent(A),
    #sum { V,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) ; -V,G : cand(k,gets(A,G)), not cand_false(k,gets(A,G)), value(A,G,V) } > 0.
:- up(k), worse(k,A).
:- up(k), not better(k,A) : agent(A).

#program beat(k).
% cex(k,alt(A,G)): the k-th counterexample, an allocation that dominates a climbed candidate.
% Line 14 of Algorithm 1: some agent who is unhappy there must be happy; for additive values,
% some agent must get strictly more than there. Sound because of the climb: an envy-free
% Pareto-efficient allocation that gave nobody more would have the counterexample's values,
% so it would dominate the candidate, and the climb had found no such allocation.
beats(k,A) :- agent(A),
    #sum { V,G : gets(A,G), value(A,G,V) ; -V,G : cex(k,alt(A,G)), value(A,G,V) } > 0.
:- not beats(k,A) : agent(A).

loop.text:
solver A = shared + abstraction + refine
solver C = shared + check          options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(alt/2))
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

loop.text:
solver A = shared + abstraction
solver C = shared + check          options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.add(G.block(M))
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

solver A = shared + abstraction + refine
solver C = shared + check          options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# Up to three dominating allocations per candidate, one rule each.
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    L = C.models(assume G(M), limit 3)
    if L.size == 0:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))
    for X in L:
        A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(alt/2))

solver A = shared + abstraction
solver C = shared + check          options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# No relevant/1: the clause is lifted from the ground programs of both ends.
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.add(G.lift(M, X))
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

variants.name: algorithm-1
variants.note: Algorithm 1 of Conati, Niskanen, de Haan and Jarvisalo (AAMAS 2025), for additive values: climb to an envy-free allocation no envy-free allocation dominates, then find any dominating allocation; the refinement: somebody gets more than there.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + abstraction + algorithm1
solver C = shared + check          options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# Algorithm 1 of Conati, Niskanen, de Haan and Jarvisalo (AAMAS 2025), for additive values, and
# enumerating every solution. A proposes an envy-free allocation (line 4). The climb (lines 7-10)
# replaces it by an envy-free allocation that dominates it, as long as there is one (each candidate
# it leaves is dominated, so it is blocked: the paper finds one solution, this loop all). C looks for
# any allocation that dominates the result (lines 11-12): none, it is a solution (line 13);
# otherwise some agent must get more than in that counterexample (line 14).
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    loop:
        A.expand(climb, cand = G(M))
        U = A.solve(assume A.atom("up", A.step))
        if not U: break
        A.add(G.block(M))      # M is dominated by U, so it is not Pareto-efficient
        M = U
        count climbs
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.expand(beat, cex = X.atoms(alt/2))     # somebody gets more than in X
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

variants.name: optimal-counterexample
variants.note: The default loop with a Pareto-optimal counterexample: of the dominating allocations, C returns one of maximum total value, so its rule removes the most.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + abstraction + refine
solver C = shared + check + welfare      options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# The default loop with a Pareto-optimal counterexample: C finds an allocation that dominates the
# candidate, of maximum total value, hence Pareto-optimal (one that dominated it would dominate the
# candidate too, with a larger total); the rule forbids every allocation it dominates.
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M), optimal)
    if X:
        A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(alt/2))     # no later candidate is dominated by X
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

variants.name: lazy-envy
variants.note: Envy-freeness as a second check: an envious pair gives a clause over the goods of the two agents; Pareto dominance as in the default loop.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + allocation + refine
solver D = shared + envy
solver C = shared + check          options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   E = A -> D via shared + glue
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# Envy-freeness lazily: A proposes any allocation; D finds an agent who envies another, and the
# clause from relevant/1 says that one of their goods must move (envy depends only on the two
# bundles). An envy-free candidate goes to the Pareto check as in the default loop.
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    Y = D.solve(assume E(M))
    if Y:
        A.add(E.clause(M, Y))                    # the envious pair: one of its goods must move
        continue
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(alt/2))     # no later candidate is dominated by X
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

variants.name: lazy-envy-optimal-counterexample
variants.note: lazy-envy with the Pareto-optimal counterexample of optimal-counterexample.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + allocation + refine
solver D = shared + envy
solver C = shared + check + welfare      options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   E = A -> D via shared + glue
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# Both: envy-freeness lazily (clauses from an envious pair), and a Pareto-optimal counterexample
# for dominance (variant optimal-counterexample).
loop:
    M = A.solve()
    if not M: stop
    Y = D.solve(assume E(M))
    if Y:
        A.add(E.clause(M, Y))
        continue
    X = C.solve(assume G(M), optimal)
    if X:
        A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(alt/2))     # no later candidate is dominated by X
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

variants.name: welfare-first
variants.note: The default loop, with candidates of the largest total value first (A.solve(optimal)).

loop.text:
solver A = shared + abstraction + refine + welfare_a
solver C = shared + check          options "--heuristic=Domain"
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# The default loop with A's candidates in order of total value (an optimal solve each time): an
# envy-free allocation of maximum total value among those left is often Pareto-optimal, so its
# check fails at once.
loop:
    M = A.solve(optimal)
    if not M: stop
    X = C.solve(assume G(M))
    if X:
        A.expand(refine, cex = X.atoms(alt/2))     # no later candidate is dominated by X
    else:
        accept M
        A.add(G.block(M))

readme:
# Project: Fair and efficient division

## Research question

An allocation of indivisible goods with additive values is envy-free (nobody values another
agent's bundle more than their own) and Pareto-efficient (no other allocation is at least as good
for everybody and better for somebody). Whether one exists is Sigma-2-complete (de Keijzer,
Bouveret, Klos and Zhang 2009), and Conati, Niskanen, de Haan and Järvisalo (2025) solve the
dichotomous case with a counterexample-guided loop of SAT calls. Which loop finds every such
allocation with the fewest refinements, and what does adapting their Algorithm 1 to additive
values buy?

## The loops

- **default**: A proposes an envy-free allocation; C finds an allocation that dominates it. Being
  dominated depends on sums, which a clause cannot say, so the refinement is a rule (Shape 3): no
  later candidate may be dominated by this counterexample (`A.expand(refine, ...)`).
- **algorithm-1**: Algorithm 1 of Conati et al. (2025), adapted from dichotomous to additive
  values. A proposes an envy-free allocation; the *climb* (lines 7–10) replaces it by an envy-free
  allocation that dominates it, as long as there is one (`A.expand(climb, ...)`, then a solve under
  the assumption `up(k)`); C looks for any allocation that dominates the result (lines 11–12). With
  none, it is a solution. Otherwise the refinement is line 14: an agent who is unhappy in the
  counterexample must be happy, which for additive values reads "some agent gets strictly more
  than in the counterexample" (`A.expand(beat, ...)`). That is stronger than "not dominated by
  it", and sound only because of the climb: an envy-free Pareto-efficient allocation that gave
  nobody more would have the counterexample's values, so it would dominate the climbed candidate.
  The paper stops at the first solution; to list them all, each candidate the climb leaves is
  blocked (it is dominated, so not Pareto-efficient).
- **optimal-counterexample**: the default loop with a Pareto-optimal counterexample: C returns a
  dominating allocation of maximum total value (`#maximize`, `C.solve(..., optimal)`). It is
  Pareto-optimal (one that dominated it would dominate the candidate too, with a larger total), so
  its rule removes the most candidates.
- **lazy-envy**: envy-freeness leaves A and becomes a second check D. An envious pair gives a
  clause from relevant/1 over the goods of the two agents (envy depends only on their two
  bundles); Pareto dominance is checked as in the default loop.
- **lazy-envy-optimal-counterexample**: lazy-envy with the counterexample of optimal-counterexample.
- **welfare-first**: the default loop with A's candidates of the largest total value first
  (`A.solve(optimal)`): such an allocation is often Pareto-optimal, so its check fails at once.
- **several**: up to three dominating allocations per candidate, one rule each.
- **lift**: no relevant/1 and no rule: the clause is lifted from the ground programs (`G.lift`).
- **reference**: the blocking loop, each refuted candidate blocked on its own.

## Baseline

Candidates / counterexamples of a run with all solutions (`node tools/bench.mjs fair-division --suite loops`;
a counterexample is a model that refuted a candidate). All loops finish each instance within 10 s;
`two-alike` has no envy-free allocation.

| instance | default | reference | several | lift | algorithm-1 | optimal-counterexample | lazy-envy | lazy-envy-optimal-counterexample | welfare-first |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| example | 6 / 3 | 11 / 0 | 5 / 4 | 8 / 5 | 10 / 2 | 5 / 2 | 1238 / 1235 | 1151 / 1148 | 5 / 2 |
| opposite-tastes | 9 / 5 | 38 / 0 | 9 / 10 | 20 / 16 | 13 / 2 | 8 / 4 | 72 / 68 | 66 / 62 | 8 / 4 |
| four-agents | 32 / 16 | 62 / 0 | 28 / 25 | 53 / 37 | 41 / 13 | 31 / 15 | 5296 / 5280 | 4975 / 4959 | 30 / 14 |
| random-1 | 22 / 10 | 95 / 0 | 17 / 9 | 46 / 34 | 30 / 4 | 18 / 6 | 9864 / 9852 | 9080 / 9068 | 18 / 6 |
| random-2 | 16 / 8 | 115 / 0 | 15 / 18 | 65 / 57 | 36 / 5 | 14 / 6 | 329 / 321 | 186 / 178 | 13 / 5 |

The rule does most of the work: the blocking loop looks at up to seven times as many candidates.
The climb of algorithm-1 needs the fewest counterexamples on the larger instances (4 on random-1
against 10 for the default loop; tied with welfare-first on random-2): most dominated candidates are left by a
cheap envy-free step instead of a check, at the price of the climb's solves (counted as
candidates) and one program part per climb step. A Pareto-optimal counterexample saves a little on
every instance. Envy-freeness is cheap to state in A and expensive to learn: the lazy loops need
hundreds to thousands of clauses, as an envy clause only rules out one pair of bundles.

## Things to try

- Combine the climb of algorithm-1 with the Pareto-optimal counterexample.
- Minimum-envy Pareto-optimal allocations when no envy-free one exists (as Conati et al. 2025 do),
  with A minimising an aggregate of the envy.
- Larger instances from the generator `additive` (suite `loops`, Campaign tab).

## References

- B. de Keijzer, S. Bouveret, T. Klos and Y. Zhang. On the complexity of efficiency and envy-freeness in fair division of indivisible goods with additive preferences. *ADT 2009*, LNCS 5783, 98–110.
- S. Bouveret and J. Lang. Efficiency and envy-freeness in fair division of indivisible goods: logical representation and complexity. *Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research* 32:525–564, 2008.
- A. Conati, A. Niskanen, R. de Haan and M. Järvisalo. Computing efficient and envy-free allocations under dichotomous preferences using SAT. *AAMAS 2025*. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3709347.3743566
